name: Marco Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good to meet you, Marco. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything here is confidential, so feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you actually think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. First thing, before boots, I check the overnight report on my phone: soil moisture probes, the weather model, and what the AI assistant thinks I should do about the wheat. We're three hundred hectares, wheat, beans and oilseed rape, plus sixty suckler cows, which are mothers raising beef calves. Dev, our stockman, does the cattle with me in the morning, and then I'm usually on the tractor with the GPS steering doing the drilling or flying the drone over the beans to look for disease.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy getting something to work that didn't before. Last spring the drone spotted a patch of rust two weeks before I'd have seen it from the ground, and that saved us maybe four thousand in spray. What wears me out is the hours in harvest, and the feeling that the companies selling us all this kit get more from our data than we do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, I still found it useful, so I'm not complaining. I'd probably post something in the farmers' group chat like, the hype's gone but the drone still spots rust. People would tease me, because I'm the one who's always first with the gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. I was half looking forward to the robot weeders, the way my dad looked forward to his first tractor with a cab. But it wouldn't change my farm. I'd keep using what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep using the AI tools every day for the spray plans and the grain marketing. I'd probably still buy the weed-mapping camera for the sprayer next year, about twelve thousand, because it already pays for itself. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Like a film that everyone said was amazing and turned out just fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think your neighbours would feel differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would be relieved. Old Bram across the road still writes his spray records in a notebook, and he'd say, see, Marco, all that money for nothing. I'd buy him a beer and tell him the notebook's lovely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about your worries over data go away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that stays. Even if AI is just a handy tool, the machinery firm still gets every yield map I've ever made. I'd keep pushing at the union for farmers to own their own data. That fight doesn't need AGI to matter.

S0.say: I'd say I still find the tools useful, so I'm not complaining. I'd post in the farmers' group chat that the hype's gone but the drone still spots rust.
S0.think: I'd be a little disappointed, because I was looking forward to robot weeders. But it wouldn't change my farm; I'd keep using what works.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily for spray plans and grain marketing. Buys a weed-mapping camera for the sprayer next year for about twelve thousand, and keeps raising farm data ownership at the union.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, like a much-hyped film that turned out just fine.
S0.quote: I was half looking forward to the robot weeders, the way my dad looked forward to his first tractor with a cab.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is the gadget farmer of his area and enjoys the role. Even in the hype-only picture he keeps his main political concern: farmers owning their own data. His neighbour Bram is the comic counterweight in his stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for farming if we get the rules right. I'd say it at the union meeting and in the group chat: robots are fine, but the data and the profits shouldn't all go to three big companies. And I'd say we need public money for retraining farm workers, not just tax breaks for machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's mostly good for me. I've got the cushion and I like the tech, so I can move early and take the gains. The danger isn't that a robot takes my job. It's that the robot works for a company that ends up owning my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy or lease a robot weeder for the beans, probably around forty thousand, and see if it cuts our spray bill. I'd put Dev through a course on running and fixing it, paid by us. And I'd join the union's working group on farm data, which I've been meaning to do for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually. A bit excited, with a little worry at the back about who ends up owning it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Dev think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's thirty-eight and smarter than he lets on. He said to me once, Marco, if a robot does the cattle, who's going to notice a cow that's off her food? He's right, and that's why he'd be the one running the machines, not replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the forty thousand come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, mostly, and we'd sell the old sprayer. We've got more than a year's costs in the bank, and Lucía's vet practice pays well, so we're not stretched. That's exactly why I can afford to go first, and I know not everyone can.

S1.say: This is good for farming if we get the rules right. Robots are fine, but the data and profits shouldn't all go to three big companies, and we need public money for retraining farm workers.
S1.think: It's mostly good for me, because I've got the cushion and like the tech. The danger isn't a robot taking my job; it's that the robot works for a company that ends up owning it.
S1.do: Buys or leases a robot weeder for the beans for about forty thousand, funded from savings and the sale of an old sprayer. Pays for Dev's training to run it and joins the union's farm data working group.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with a small worry about who ends up owning it all.
S1.quote: The danger isn't that a robot takes my job. It's that the robot works for a company that ends up owning my job.
S1.fieldNote: Marco is open about the fact that his savings and his partner's income let him move first, and he says plainly that not everyone can. His concern is ownership and power, not his own job. He sees Dev as the operator of the machines rather than their victim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's speed things up a lot. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, publicly, that this is too fast and the government has to act now. I'd want a law that says farm data belongs to farmers, a tax on the robot companies' profits, and a basic income for people who lose work. I'd say it on the radio if they asked, and they might, because I'm the AI guy round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my farm would probably be fine. I could buy robots quicker than most. What scares me is the investment funds buying up every farm around me and running them from a screen in another country. Two years isn't long enough for anyone to stop that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast. In the first six months I'd buy the robots I'd been eyeing, probably a hundred thousand, half from savings and half on a loan, so we stay competitive. I'd get Dev certified to supervise the whole fleet. And I'd help set up an emergency group in the union to lobby for the data law and against land sales to funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not scared for my own family, but I'd feel like I was watching the village change from the cab of a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pablo writes software in the city, so he'd be in the firing line before me. I'd tell him to come home if he needed to, there's a room and there's work. Inés is studying agronomy, which is crop science, and I'd tell her to finish, because someone still has to decide what to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd borrow fifty thousand with only two years' warning. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. If everything goes robot, machines will get cheaper fast, and I'd be the idiot who bought at the top. But if I wait, the funds buy the land next door and I can't compete. I'd rather be the idiot with a robot than the idiot without one.

S2.say: This is too fast and the government has to act now. I'd want a law that farm data belongs to farmers, a tax on robot company profits and a basic income for people who lose work.
S2.think: My farm would probably be fine because I can buy robots quicker than most. What scares me is investment funds buying up the farms around me and running them from a screen abroad.
S2.do: Buys about a hundred thousand of robots within six months, half from savings and half borrowed. Gets Dev certified to supervise the fleet and sets up a union emergency group to lobby for a data law and against land sales to funds.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not for his family but for the village, which he'd watch change from the cab of a robot.
S2.quote: What scares me is the investment funds buying up every farm around me and running them from a screen in another country.
S2.fieldNote: Even at two years, Marco's personal position looks safe to him; his fear is about investment funds and remote ownership. He admits borrowing to buy fast could be a mistake, but sees standing still as worse. He'd invite his son home if software work vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd say this is the window to set the rules. I'd push the union to get a farm-data law and land-sale rules passed in the first two years, before the machines are everywhere. I'd say farmers who are scared should talk to the ones who've already tried the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can do it properly, not in a panic. I'd be sixty-three when it fully lands, which is about when I'd want to step back anyway. So the timing suits me, as long as the rules come first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy robots in stages, one machine a year, and only once the last one paid for itself, so no big loan. I'd run a free open day twice a year for the neighbours to see the kit working. I'd rather Bram laughs at my robot in my yard than buys a worse one off a salesman. And I'd start talking to Inés about taking over the arable side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Five years is enough to be clever about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the open days?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the worst thing that happens in farming is everyone making the same mistake on their own. If twenty of us see what works and what breaks, we can buy smarter, maybe even buy together. It's what the old discussion groups used to do with grass and fertiliser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does this compare with the two-year one for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years makes me borrow and shout. Five makes me plan and teach. The end is the same, but in this one I keep my blood pressure.

S3.say: This is the window to set the rules: a farm-data law and land-sale rules in the first two years. Farmers who are scared should talk to the ones who've already tried the kit.
S3.think: I can do it properly, not in a panic. I'd be sixty-three when it lands, about when I want to step back anyway, so the timing suits me if the rules come first.
S3.do: Buys robots in stages, one machine a year and only once the last has paid for itself, with no big loan. Runs free open days twice a year for neighbours and starts talking with his daughter about taking over the arable side.
S3.feel: Calm; five years is enough to be clever about it.
S3.quote: I'd rather Bram laughs at my robot in my yard than buys a worse one off a salesman.
S3.fieldNote: Marco sums up the difference in warning time neatly: two years makes him 'borrow and shout', five makes him 'plan and teach'. The open days show his instinct to share knowledge. Succession to his daughter becomes part of the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get this right, so there's no excuse. I'd keep pushing at the union for public research farms that test robots and share the results freely. I'd say we should be training young people now for the jobs that run alongside the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's the most comfortable one. By 2036 I'll be sixty-eight, and I'd love to see Inés running a robot farm that I helped her set up. My worry is only whether the rules get written by us or by the companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on adding one machine a year, like in the five-year one, and keep the open days. I'd work with Inés on a handover plan over about seven years, with her running more each season. And I'd put a little of our savings into a farmer-owned machinery co-op if the union started one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite hopeful. A bit wistful for the old ways, but not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss anything about farming the old way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being tired in a good way. When you've been on the combine fourteen hours and you smell of diesel and dust, and you sit on the step with a cup of tea. If the robot does the combining, I lose that. I'd miss it more than I'd admit to Bram.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lucía say about your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say make sure you actually retire this time. She's heard me say I'm stepping back three times already. I'd tell her the robots will make sure of it.

S4.say: Ten years is enough to get this right, so there's no excuse. We need public research farms that test robots and share results freely, and training for young people now.
S4.think: It's the most comfortable one for me. I'd love to see my daughter running a robot farm I helped her set up, as long as the rules are written by us and not the companies.
S4.do: Keeps adding one machine a year and runs the open days. Works out a seven-year handover with Inés and puts some savings into a farmer-owned machinery co-op if the union starts one.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, with a small wistfulness for the old ways.
S4.quote: By 2036 I'll be sixty-eight, and I'd love to see Inés running a robot farm that I helped her set up.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years is Marco's ideal case: he gets to hand a modern farm to his daughter. His only nostalgia is for being tired in a good way after a long harvest day. His political worry, who writes the rules, never goes away in any scenario.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, the two-year one. Not for my farm, but because the investment funds would hoover up land before anyone could write a rule. What would help is a law saying farm data belongs to the farmer, limits on funds buying farmland, and public money for farmer-owned machine co-ops.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who fixes the robots. Everyone pictures a shiny machine in a field, but the real question is whether the mechanic lives in our village or on a server somewhere. That decides whether the money stays here.

headlineQuote: Everyone pictures a shiny machine in a field, but the real question is whether the mechanic lives in our village or on a server somewhere.
portrait: Marco Reyes, 58, farms three hundred hectares of wheat, beans and oilseed rape with a sixty-cow suckler herd, and is the local early adopter: GPS steering, a scouting drone and AI tools every day. He's left-leaning and worries far more about corporate and investment-fund control of farming than about his own job. With strong savings and a vet partner's income, he can afford to move first and says so openly. Two years of warning makes him 'borrow and shout'; five or ten let him 'plan and teach', with open days for neighbours and a handover to his daughter Inés.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because investment funds would buy up farmland before any rules could be written.
whatWouldHelp: A law that farm data belongs to farmers, limits on funds buying farmland and public money for farmer-owned machinery co-ops.
